articles.title: The blueprint for single-use biomanufacturing facilities
articles.text:
Articles The blueprint for single-use biomanufacturing facilities Stainless steel is strong, but flexibility is faster. Here is how single-use technology is rewriting the economics of biopharmaceutical facility design Written by Trevor J Henderson Trevor J Henderson Trevor Henderson is the Creative Services Director for the Laboratory Products Group at LabX Media Group. With over two decades of experience, he specializes in scientific and technical writing, editing, View Full Profile Learn about our Editorial Policies . Jun 4, 2026 | 8 min read A well-designed single-use biomanufacturing facility eliminates stainless steel vessels and CIP/SIP infrastructure, replacing fixed equipment with disposable assemblies that can be staged, configured, and changed over between product campaigns in hours rather than days. Flow (2026) Download PDF Register for free to listen to this article Listen with Speechify 0:00 8:00 Highlights in this article Single-use vs. stainless steel: the facility design decision Facility layout and design principles Upstream architecture: from seed train to production bioreactor Downstream integration in a single-use facility Commissioning and qualification timelines Supply chain design for single-use operations For the better part of five decades, stainless steel was the only credible architecture for commercial biopharmaceutical manufacturing. Fixed vessels, welded piping, clean-in-place and steam-in-place infrastructure, and facility timelines measured in years were simply the cost of entry into GMP production. The capital requirements were prohibitive for all but the most well-capitalized manufacturers, and the facilities that existed were built to run a single product at high volume for the lifetime of a commercial approval. The economics have shifted fundamentally. For facilities targeting clinical and early commercial scale, manufacturing multiple products across a shared infrastructure, or responding to the compressed timelines of modern drug development, single-use architecture has become the default design choice. The question for most new biopharmaceutical facility projects is no longer whether to use single-use technology, but how to design a facility that maximizes what single-use makes possible. The transition to single-use carries real and measurable operational advantages: lower capital commitment, faster commissioning, superior multi-product flexibility, and the elimination of cleaning validation as an ongoing operational burden. It also creates design requirements, supply chain obligations, and regulatory considerations specific to the disposable format. This guide covers the architecture, qualification approach, and operational design of a well-executed single-use biomanufacturing facility. For a broader view of bioprocessing scale-up and the manufacturing technologies shaping the industry, see the ultimate guide to bioprocessing scale-up and Pharma 4.0 . Continue reading below... Articles Improving HLA-informed cell therapy development Explore engineered cellular models and screening approaches designed to support more targeted evaluation of adoptive cell therapies. Read More Single-use vs. stainless steel: the facility design decision The choice between single-use and stainless steel architecture is a financial and operational decision as much as a technical one. The table below maps the key decision factors across both platforms, using the dimensions most relevant to facility design, commissioning, and long-term operations. Factor Single-use Stainless steel Facility capital cost Lower; eliminates CIP/SIP systems, stainless vessel fabrication, and GMP piping runs Higher upfront investment; appropriate where sustained high-volume production justifies the fixed asset Commissioning timeline 12 to 18 months faster than equivalent stainless facility; no CIP/SIP installation or cleaning validation required Longer timeline; CIP/SIP system installation, verification, and cleaning validation are significant commissioning activities Cleaning validation Eliminated; disposable format removes inter-product carryover concern for product-contact surfaces Required for each product-contact surface; must be repeated and revalidated for new products or cleaning agent changes Multi-product flexibility High; changeover between product campaigns requires staging new single-use assemblies rather than cleaning and revalidating fixed equipment Lower; cleaning validation is product-specific and limits the speed and economics of campaign changeover Per-run consumables cost High; bags, tubing sets, filters, and sterile connectors are replaced with each production run Low per run; hardware is reused with cleaning and sterilization between campaigns Supply chain risk Higher; production continuity depends on qualified single-use component supply from a limited supplier base Lower; relies on in-house utilities and reusable hardware with manageable spare parts exposure Best fit Clinical-scale and early commercial production; multi-product facilities; programs requiring fast facility deployment High-volume commercial manufacture of single products; facilities where annual consumables spend would exceed the stainless capital advantage Facility layout and design principles Single-use biomanufacturing requires a different approach to facility layout than stainless steel design. The absence of CIP/SIP utility connections eliminates major constraints on room placement and piping routing, giving facility designers more flexibility in configuring production spaces. But single-use introduces its own spatial requirements, particularly around component staging and storage, that are frequently underestimated in facility planning. Cleanroom classification and environmental control The classified area requirements for a single-use biomanufacturing suite depend on whether the process uses open or closed systems at each step. Fully closed single-use assemblies, where all fluid paths are sealed and connections are made through sterile connectors rather than open-air manipulations, can be operated in ISO Class 8 (Grade D) environments for most operations. Steps involving open product contact, such as open-system sampling or aseptic connections not conducted inside an isolator or laminar flow hood, require ISO Class 7 (Grade C) conditions or better. Designing for closed-system operation throughout the production suite maximizes the facility area that can be classified at Grade D rather than Grade C or B, reducing both the capital cost and the operational overhead of maintaining higher-classification environments. Facility designers should map each process step against its containment status before defining cleanroom classification requirements for each room. Component staging and storage Single-use facilities require substantially more staging and storage space adjacent to production areas than stainless steel facilities of equivalent production capacity. Bioreactor bags, tubing sets, filter capsules, sterile connectors, and other components must be stored under controlled conditions, transported to the point of use, inspected for integrity before use, and staged for installation. A 1,000-liter single-use production campaign may consume hundreds of individual single-use components. Allocating adequate staging space within or immediately adjacent to the production suite is a facility design decision with direct operational consequences. Utility requirements Single-use facilities still require utilities, but at a substantially different scale and configuration than stainless steel facilities. Purified water and water for injection remain necessary for buffer and media preparation, formulation, and cleaning of reusable equipment. Compressed gas delivery (nitrogen, air, carbon dioxide, oxygen) is required for bioreactor sparging and process control. Clean steam, if present at all, serves a more limited role than in stainless steel facilities. The elimination of CIP/SIP systems removes the large hot water, caustic, and steam utility loads that dominate stainless steel utility design. Continue reading below... Articles DNA synthesis 101: steps, enzymes, and importance Explore the principles, technologies, and applications that enable scientists to design and build DNA for research, biotechnology, and therapeutic development. Read More Upstream architecture: from seed train to production bioreactor The upstream design of a single-use facility defines the path from cell bank vial to production bioreactor, through a series of expansion steps that progressively increase culture volume while maintaining cell health and viability. Single-use bioreactors are available across the full range of volumes used in clinical and commercial manufacturing, from two-liter development systems to 2,000-liter production bioreactors, making fully single-use seed train design achievable for most applications. Seed train design A single-use seed train progresses the culture through increasing vessel volumes, with each stage timed to deliver cells at the target density and viability for inoculation of the next vessel. The table below illustrates a representative single-use seed train configuration for a 1,000-liter fed-batch production run. Stage Typical volume Single-use system type Duration Vial thaw and shake flask expansion 50 mL to 3L Shake flasks or small-scale wave bioreactor 7 to 14 days from thaw to target density for inoculation N-4 / N-3 expansion 3 to 15L Single-use rocking bioreactor or small stirred-tank 3 to 5 days per stage N-2 seed bioreactor 50 to 100L Single-use stirred-tank bioreactor 3 to 5 days N-1 seed bioreactor 100 to 250L Single-use stirred-tank bioreactor; perfusion capable if N-1 perfusion strategy is used 3 to 7 days (longer in perfusion mode) Production bioreactor 500 to 2,000L Single-use stirred-tank bioreactor 10 to 14 days (fed-batch) or 30 to 90 days (perfusion) N-1 perfusion, running the final seed train stage in perfusion mode to achieve higher viable cell density at inoculation of the production bioreactor, is an increasingly common design choice for single-use facilities targeting process intensification. Commissioning and qualification timelines The commissioning timeline advantage of single-use facilities is one of the most frequently cited arguments for the platform, and the advantage is real. Eliminating CIP/SIP systems removes the installation, qualification, and cleaning validation work that represents weeks to months of commissioning time in stainless steel facilities. A well-planned single-use facility can move from equipment delivery to first GMP production run in 12 to 18 months less than an equivalent stainless steel facility. Qualification of single-use equipment follows the same IQ/OQ/PQ framework that applies to all GMP production equipment. The hardware platform, including the bioreactor controller, drive system, sensors, and process piping connections, requires full IQ/OQ/PQ qualification. Bag integrity testing for each individual production bag, confirming the absence of leaks before inoculation, is a per-run pre-use check rather than a qualification activity, but the procedure for conducting it must be established during qualification. Leachables and extractables (L&E) testing is a commissioning requirement specific to single-use systems. All product-contact single-use components must be characterized for chemical entities that can leach from the plastic into the drug substance under process conditions. Major bioprocessing equipment suppliers publish extractables characterization packages for their single-use component portfolios, but sponsors are responsible for demonstrating that the extractables profile of each component is compatible with their specific drug substance under their specific process conditions. Read More Supply chain design for single-use operations The COVID-19 pandemic demonstrated at scale what single-use manufacturing experts had long understood: a facility whose production continuity depends on a single qualified supplier for critical single-use components is carrying supply chain risk that does not appear on its balance sheet until a shortage makes it visible. Bag availability constraints and sterile connector shortages disrupted biopharmaceutical manufacturing timelines across the industry in 2021 and 2022, affecting programs ranging from COVID-19 vaccine manufacturing to standard clinical-phase biologics production. Designing supply chain resilience into a single-use facility requires decisions made before production begins. Component standardization, reducing the number of unique single-use assembly configurations to the minimum required for the production operations, simplifies inventory management and expands the range of suppliers capable of meeting specifications. Dual-source qualification, maintaining two qualified suppliers for each critical single-use component, provides an alternative supply path when primary supplier availability is constrained. Safety stock, maintaining a defined weeks-of-supply inventory for critical components at site, provides a buffer against short-term supply disruptions. The BioPhorum industry consortium has published specific guidance on single-use supply chain risk management, including qualification frameworks for supplier assessment, component standardization strategies, and supply continuity planning approaches. Facilities designing their single-use supply chain should engage with current industry guidance rather than developing resilience strategies independently. Supplier qualification for single-use components in GMP manufacturing requires assessing not only component performance but the supplier's quality management system, change notification practices, and manufacturing site audit history. A supplier that implements a change to film formulation, component design, or manufacturing process without adequate notification can create an uncontrolled change in the drug manufacturer's validated system, triggering requalification obligations and potential regulatory reporting requirements. This article was produced under Drug Discovery News' AI Editorial Guidelines Download PDF Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) What is a single-use biomanufacturing facility? A single-use biomanufacturing facility is a GMP pharmaceutical production facility in which the equipment that contacts the drug substance during manufacturing, including bioreactor vessels, tubing, filters, mixing containers, and storage bags, uses disposable components that are replaced with each production run rather than cleaned and reused. Single-use facilities eliminate the need for clean-in-place and steam-in-place systems and the cleaning validation required for stainless steel equipment, offering lower capital cost, faster commissioning, and greater flexibility for multi-product manufacturing. How does a single-use facility compare to a stainless steel facility in terms of cost? Single-use facilities require significantly lower upfront capital investment than equivalent stainless steel facilities, primarily because they eliminate the cost of CIP/SIP systems, stainless steel vessel fabrication, and GMP piping infrastructure. They also commission 12 to 18 months faster. The trade-off is higher ongoing operational expenditure: bags, tubing sets, filters, and sterile connectors are replaced with each production run, creating a consumables cost that accumulates over time. For clinical-scale and early commercial facilities, the capital savings and commissioning speed of single-use typically outweigh the consumables cost premium. At very high commercial volumes, the calculation shifts toward stainless steel. What are the main components of a single-use biomanufacturing facility? The core production equipment in a single-use biomanufacturing facility includes single-use bioreactors at each stage of the seed train and production, single-use mixing systems for buffer and media preparation, single-use filtration assemblies for harvest clarification and sterile filtration, single-use tangential flow filtration systems for ultrafiltration and diafiltration, and single-use storage bags for in-process and drug substance hold. Connecting all of these components are single-use tubing assemblies and sterile connectors that maintain closed-system fluid paths throughout the manufacturing process. What are leachables and extractables in single-use bioprocessing? Extractables are chemical compounds that can be released from a single-use material under aggressive laboratory extraction conditions. Leachables are the subset of those compounds that actually migrate into the drug product under normal process conditions during manufacturing. Both categories must be characterized for all product-contact single-use components as part of the regulatory submission for a biologic drug. Bioprocessing equipment suppliers publish extractables characterization packages for their single-use component portfolios, and drug manufacturers are responsible for demonstrating that the identified compounds are present at levels that pose no risk to product safety or patient safety. Feb 18, 2026 | 2 min read credit: istock.com/Noctiluxx Download PDF ATLANTA, GA, February 18th, 2026 --( BUSINESS WIRE )--Axion BioSystems today announced that the FDA's Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER) has accepted the company’s letter of intent (LOI) into the Innovative Science and Technology Approaches for New Drugs (ISTAND) Program for its Human iPSC-Cardiomyocyte MEA Assay for Prediction of Clinical Cardiovascular Repolarization Risk. The submission represents the first stem cell-derived, functional cardiac safety assay accepted into the ISTAND program. The ISTAND program is designed to advance promising, high-impact New Approach Methodologies (NAMs) through structured FDA engagement to inform regulatory decision-making. Acceptance of Axion’s LOI reflects the FDA’s interest in advancing mature, human-relevant, non-animal strategies that can strengthen early assessment of clinical cardiac risk. Cardiac safety remains a major challenge, contributing both to late-stage failures and, in some cases, the premature discontinuation of otherwise promising therapies. The proposed assay combines human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes (hiPSC-CMs) with Axion’s Maestro multielectrode array (MEA) technology to measure cardiac electrophysiology across a multicellular network, or syncytium. Using label-free, noninvasive recordings, the assay enables detection of delayed repolarization, beat-to-beat variability, and arrhythmia-like events associated with proarrhythmic risk — providing human-relevant functional insight beyond single-ion-channel or animal-based approaches. Standardized implementation of the assay is enabled by Axion’s Maestro MEA platform, a widely adopted electrophysiology tool designed to support scalable, reproducible workflows in pharmaceutical and CRO environments. Maestro enables simultaneous recording across up to 96 wells with integrated environmental control, automation-ready operation, and multimodal capabilities. These features support consistent application of the hiPSC-CM MEA assay in regulatory-facing cardiac safety evaluations intended to inform decision-making. “Acceptance into the FDA’s ISTAND Program is an important milestone, not just for Axion BioSystems, but for the broader movement toward human-relevant cardiac safety assessment,” said Julien Bradley , CEO of Axion BioSystems. “This assay reflects more than a decade of scientific validation, collaborative studies, and real-world use across industry and regulatory settings. We look forward to working with FDA to advance its qualification as a drug development tool that can increase confidence in early cardiac safety decisions.” Axion has long played a key role in advancing functional cardiac safety assays, including participation in multicenter initiatives such as the Comprehensive in vitro Proarrhythmia Assay (CiPA). These efforts helped demonstrate that hiPSC-cardiomyocyte MEA assays can reliably identify delayed repolarization and arrhythmia-like events associated with torsades de pointes risk, contributing to their growing use in regulatory-facing drug development programs. As part of the ISTAND program, Axion BioSystems will engage with FDA to develop a Qualification Plan defining the assay’s context of use, analytical validation strategy, and supporting evidence. Qualification of the assay as a DDT may enable broader regulatory acceptance of stem cell-derived functional cardiac safety data across drug development programs. Fixed vessels, welded piping, clean-in-place and steam-in-place infrastructure, and facility timelines measured in years were simply the cost of entry into GMP production. The capital requirements were prohibitive for all but the most well-capitalized manufacturers, and the facilities that existed were built to run a single product at high volume for the lifetime of a commercial approval. The economics have shifted fundamentally. For facilities targeting clinical and early commercial scale, manufacturing multiple products across a shared infrastructure, or responding to the compressed timelines of modern drug development, single-use architecture has become the default design choice. The question for most new biopharmaceutical facility projects is no longer whether to use single-use technology, but how to design a facility that maximizes what single-use makes possible. The transition to single-use carries real and measurable operational advantages: lower capital commitment, faster commissioning, superior multi-product flexibility, and the elimination of cleaning validation as an ongoing operational burden. It also creates design requirements, supply chain obligations, and regulatory considerations specific to the disposable format. This guide covers the architecture, qualification approach, and operational design of a well-executed single-use biomanufacturing facility. Read More Single-use vs. stainless steel: the facility design decision The choice between single-use and stainless steel architecture is a financial and operational decision as much as a technical one. The table below maps the key decision factors across both platforms, using the dimensions most relevant to facility design, commissioning, and long-term operations. Factor Single-use Stainless steel Facility capital cost Lower; eliminates CIP/SIP systems, stainless vessel fabrication, and GMP piping runs Higher upfront investment; appropriate where sustained high-volume production justifies the fixed asset Commissioning timeline 12 to 18 months faster than equivalent stainless facility; no CIP/SIP installation or cleaning validation required Longer timeline; CIP/SIP system installation, verification, and cleaning validation are significant commissioning activities Cleaning validation Eliminated; disposable format removes inter-product carryover concern for product-contact surfaces Required for each product-contact surface; must be repeated and revalidated for new products or cleaning agent changes Multi-product flexibility High; changeover between product campaigns requires staging new single-use assemblies rather than cleaning and revalidating fixed equipment Lower; cleaning validation is product-specific and limits the speed and economics of campaign changeover Per-run consumables cost High; bags, tubing sets, filters, and sterile connectors are replaced with each production run Low per run; hardware is reused with cleaning and sterilization between campaigns Supply chain risk Higher; production continuity depends on qualified single-use component supply from a limited supplier base Lower; relies on in-house utilities and reusable hardware with manageable spare parts exposure Best fit Clinical-scale and early commercial production; multi-product facilities; programs requiring fast facility deployment High-volume commercial manufacture of single products; facilities where annual consumables spend would exceed the stainless capital advantage Facility layout and design principles Single-use biomanufacturing requires a different approach to facility layout than stainless steel design. The absence of CIP/SIP utility connections eliminates major constraints on room placement and piping routing, giving facility designers more flexibility in configuring production spaces. But single-use introduces its own spatial requirements, particularly around component staging and storage, that are frequently underestimated in facility planning. Cleanroom classification and environmental control The classified area requirements for a single-use biomanufacturing suite depend on whether the process uses open or closed systems at each step. Fully closed single-use assemblies, where all fluid paths are sealed and connections are made through sterile connectors rather than open-air manipulations, can be operated in ISO Class 8 (Grade D) environments for most operations. Steps involving open product contact, such as open-system sampling or aseptic connections not conducted inside an isolator or laminar flow hood, require ISO Class 7 (Grade C) conditions or better. Designing for closed-system operation throughout the production suite maximizes the facility area that can be classified at Grade D rather than Grade C or B, reducing both the capital cost and the operational overhead of maintaining higher-classification environments. Facility designers should map each process step against its containment status before defining cleanroom classification requirements for each room. Component staging and storage Single-use facilities require substantially more staging and storage space adjacent to production areas than stainless steel facilities of equivalent production capacity. Bioreactor bags, tubing sets, filter capsules, sterile connectors, and other components must be stored under controlled conditions, transported to the point of use, inspected for integrity before use, and staged for installation. A 1,000-liter single-use production campaign may consume hundreds of individual single-use components. Allocating adequate staging space within or immediately adjacent to the production suite is a facility design decision with direct operational consequences. Utility requirements Single-use facilities still require utilities, but at a substantially different scale and configuration than stainless steel facilities. Purified water and water for injection remain necessary for buffer and media preparation, formulation, and cleaning of reusable equipment. Compressed gas delivery (nitrogen, air, carbon dioxide, oxygen) is required for bioreactor sparging and process control. Clean steam, if present at all, serves a more limited role than in stainless steel facilities. The elimination of CIP/SIP systems removes the large hot water, caustic, and steam utility loads that dominate stainless steel utility design. Continue reading below... Component standardization, reducing the number of unique single-use assembly configurations to the minimum required for the production operations, simplifies inventory management and expands the range of suppliers capable of meeting specifications. Dual-source qualification, maintaining two qualified suppliers for each critical single-use component, provides an alternative supply path when primary supplier availability is constrained. Safety stock, maintaining a defined weeks-of-supply inventory for critical components at site, provides a buffer against short-term supply disruptions. The BioPhorum industry consortium has published specific guidance on single-use supply chain risk management, including qualification frameworks for supplier assessment, component standardization strategies, and supply continuity planning approaches. Facilities designing their single-use supply chain should engage with current industry guidance rather than developing resilience strategies independently. Supplier qualification for single-use components in GMP manufacturing requires assessing not only component performance but the supplier's quality management system, change notification practices, and manufacturing site audit history. A supplier that implements a change to film formulation, component design, or manufacturing process without adequate notification can create an uncontrolled change in the drug manufacturer's validated system, triggering requalification obligations and potential regulatory reporting requirements. A single-use biomanufacturing facility is a GMP pharmaceutical production facility in which the equipment that contacts the drug substance during manufacturing, including bioreactor vessels, tubing, filters, mixing containers, and storage bags, uses disposable components that are replaced with each production run rather than cleaned and reused. Single-use facilities eliminate the need for clean-in-place and steam-in-place systems and the cleaning validation required for stainless steel equipment, offering lower capital cost, faster commissioning, and greater flexibility for multi-product manufacturing. How does a single-use facility compare to a stainless steel facility in terms of cost? Single-use facilities require significantly lower upfront capital investment than equivalent stainless steel facilities, primarily because they eliminate the cost of CIP/SIP systems, stainless steel vessel fabrication, and GMP piping infrastructure. They also commission 12 to 18 months faster. The trade-off is higher ongoing operational expenditure: bags, tubing sets, filters, and sterile connectors are replaced with each production run, creating a consumables cost that accumulates over time. For clinical-scale and early commercial facilities, the capital savings and commissioning speed of single-use typically outweigh the consumables cost premium. At very high commercial volumes, the calculation shifts toward stainless steel. What are the main components of a single-use biomanufacturing facility? The core production equipment in a single-use biomanufacturing facility includes single-use bioreactors at each stage of the seed train and production, single-use mixing systems for buffer and media preparation, single-use filtration assemblies for harvest clarification and sterile filtration, single-use tangential flow filtration systems for ultrafiltration and diafiltration, and single-use storage bags for in-process and drug substance hold. Connecting all of these components are single-use tubing assemblies and sterile connectors that maintain closed-system fluid paths throughout the manufacturing process. What are leachables and extractables in single-use bioprocessing? Extractables are chemical compounds that can be released from a single-use material under aggressive laboratory extraction conditions. Leachables are the subset of those compounds that actually migrate into the drug product under normal process conditions during manufacturing. Both categories must be characterized for all product-contact single-use components as part of the regulatory submission for a biologic drug. Bioprocessing equipment suppliers publish extractables characterization packages for their single-use component portfolios, and drug manufacturers are responsible for demonstrating that the identified compounds are present at levels that pose no risk to product safety or patient safety. The submission represents the first stem cell-derived, functional cardiac safety assay accepted into the ISTAND program. Acceptance of Axion’s LOI reflects the FDA’s interest in advancing mature, human-relevant, non-animal strategies that can strengthen early assessment of clinical cardiac risk. Cardiac safety remains a major challenge, contributing both to late-stage failures and, in some cases, the premature discontinuation of otherwise promising therapies. The proposed assay combines human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes (hiPSC-CMs) with Axion’s Maestro multielectrode array (MEA) technology to measure cardiac electrophysiology across a multicellular network, or syncytium. Using label-free, noninvasive recordings, the assay enables detection of delayed repolarization, beat-to-beat variability, and arrhythmia-like events associated with proarrhythmic risk — providing human-relevant functional insight beyond single-ion-channel or animal-based approaches. Standardized implementation of the assay is enabled by Axion’s Maestro MEA platform, a widely adopted electrophysiology tool designed to support scalable, reproducible workflows in pharmaceutical and CRO environments. Maestro enables simultaneous recording across up to 96 wells with integrated environmental control, automation-ready operation, and multimodal capabilities. These features support consistent application of the hiPSC-CM MEA assay in regulatory-facing cardiac safety evaluations intended to inform decision-making. “Acceptance into the FDA’s ISTAND Program is an important milestone, not just for Axion BioSystems, but for the broader movement toward human-relevant cardiac safety assessment,” said Julien Bradley , CEO of Axion BioSystems. “This assay reflects more than a decade of scientific validation, collaborative studies, and real-world use across industry and regulatory settings. These efforts helped demonstrate that hiPSC-cardiomyocyte MEA assays can reliably identify delayed repolarization and arrhythmia-like events associated with torsades de pointes risk, contributing to their growing use in regulatory-facing drug development programs. As part of the ISTAND program, Axion BioSystems will engage with FDA to develop a Qualification Plan defining the assay’s context of use, analytical validation strategy, and supporting evidence. Qualification of the assay as a DDT may enable broader regulatory acceptance of stem cell-derived functional cardiac safety data across drug development programs. Read More Single-use vs. stainless steel: the facility design decision The choice between single-use and stainless steel architecture is a financial and operational decision as much as a technical one. The table below maps the key decision factors across both platforms, using the dimensions most relevant to facility design, commissioning, and long-term operations. Factor Single-use Stainless steel Facility capital cost Lower; eliminates CIP/SIP systems, stainless vessel fabrication, and GMP piping runs Higher upfront investment; appropriate where sustained high-volume production justifies the fixed asset Commissioning timeline 12 to 18 months faster than equivalent stainless facility; no CIP/SIP installation or cleaning validation required Longer timeline; CIP/SIP system installation, verification, and cleaning validation are significant commissioning activities Cleaning validation Eliminated; disposable format removes inter-product carryover concern for product-contact surfaces Required for each product-contact surface; must be repeated and revalidated for new products or cleaning agent changes Multi-product flexibility High; changeover between product campaigns requires staging new single-use assemblies rather than cleaning and revalidating fixed equipment Lower; cleaning validation is product-specific and limits the speed and economics of campaign changeover Per-run consumables cost High; bags, tubing sets, filters, and sterile connectors are replaced with each production run Low per run; hardware is reused with cleaning and sterilization between campaigns Supply chain risk Higher; production continuity depends on qualified single-use component supply from a limited supplier base Lower; relies on in-house utilities and reusable hardware with manageable spare parts exposure Best fit Clinical-scale and early commercial production; multi-product facilities; programs requiring fast facility deployment High-volume commercial manufacture of single products; facilities where annual consumables spend would exceed the stainless capital advantage Facility layout and design principles Single-use biomanufacturing requires a different approach to facility layout than stainless steel design. The absence of CIP/SIP utility connections eliminates major constraints on room placement and piping routing, giving facility designers more flexibility in configuring production spaces. But single-use introduces its own spatial requirements, particularly around component staging and storage, that are frequently underestimated in facility planning. Cleanroom classification and environmental control The classified area requirements for a single-use biomanufacturing suite depend on whether the process uses open or closed systems at each step. Fully closed single-use assemblies, where all fluid paths are sealed and connections are made through sterile connectors rather than open-air manipulations, can be operated in ISO Class 8 (Grade D) environments for most operations. Steps involving open product contact, such as open-system sampling or aseptic connections not conducted inside an isolator or laminar flow hood, require ISO Class 7 (Grade C) conditions or better. Designing for closed-system operation throughout the production suite maximizes the facility area that can be classified at Grade D rather than Grade C or B, reducing both the capital cost and the operational overhead of maintaining higher-classification environments. Facility designers should map each process step against its containment status before defining cleanroom classification requirements for each room. Component staging and storage Single-use facilities require substantially more staging and storage space adjacent to production areas than stainless steel facilities of equivalent production capacity. Bioreactor bags, tubing sets, filter capsules, sterile connectors, and other components must be stored under controlled conditions, transported to the point of use, inspected for integrity before use, and staged for installation. A 1,000-liter single-use production campaign may consume hundreds of individual single-use components. Allocating adequate staging space within or immediately adjacent to the production suite is a facility design decision with direct operational consequences. Utility requirements Single-use facilities still require utilities, but at a substantially different scale and configuration than stainless steel facilities. Purified water and water for injection remain necessary for buffer and media preparation, formulation, and cleaning of reusable equipment. Compressed gas delivery (nitrogen, air, carbon dioxide, oxygen) is required for bioreactor sparging and process control. Clean steam, if present at all, serves a more limited role than in stainless steel facilities. The elimination of CIP/SIP systems removes the large hot water, caustic, and steam utility loads that dominate stainless steel utility design. Continue reading below... Read More Upstream architecture: from seed train to production bioreactor The upstream design of a single-use facility defines the path from cell bank vial to production bioreactor, through a series of expansion steps that progressively increase culture volume while maintaining cell health and viability. Single-use bioreactors are available across the full range of volumes used in clinical and commercial manufacturing, from two-liter development systems to 2,000-liter production bioreactors, making fully single-use seed train design achievable for most applications. Seed train design A single-use seed train progresses the culture through increasing vessel volumes, with each stage timed to deliver cells at the target density and viability for inoculation of the next vessel. The table below illustrates a representative single-use seed train configuration for a 1,000-liter fed-batch production run. Stage Typical volume Single-use system type Duration Vial thaw and shake flask expansion 50 mL to 3L Shake flasks or small-scale wave bioreactor 7 to 14 days from thaw to target density for inoculation N-4 / N-3 expansion 3 to 15L Single-use rocking bioreactor or small stirred-tank 3 to 5 days per stage N-2 seed bioreactor 50 to 100L Single-use stirred-tank bioreactor 3 to 5 days N-1 seed bioreactor 100 to 250L Single-use stirred-tank bioreactor; perfusion capable if N-1 perfusion strategy is used 3 to 7 days (longer in perfusion mode) Production bioreactor 500 to 2,000L Single-use stirred-tank bioreactor 10 to 14 days (fed-batch) or 30 to 90 days (perfusion) N-1 perfusion, running the final seed train stage in perfusion mode to achieve higher viable cell density at inoculation of the production bioreactor, is an increasingly common design choice for single-use facilities targeting process intensification. By increasing the inoculum VCD from 10 to 20 million cells per milliliter in standard fed-batch seed trains to 50 million cells per milliliter or higher in perfusion seed trains, N-1 perfusion can reduce production bioreactor run time or increase production bioreactor inoculation density without requiring the production bioreactor itself to operate in perfusion mode. Production bioreactor selection Production bioreactor selection for a single-use facility requires matching the vessel volume, geometric design, and control system capabilities to the process requirements. Key selection criteria include the oxygen transfer coefficient (kLa) achievable at the target agitation speed and gassing rate, the mixing time at maximum working volume, the range of temperature, pH, and dissolved oxygen control, and the control system architecture and its compatibility with process analytical technology (PAT) sensors. Single-use bioreactors are available from all major bioprocessing equipment suppliers in standard volume configurations. Most commercial single-use production bioreactors at 200 liters and above use cylindrical stirred-tank designs with bottom-mounted or top-mounted impellers and submerged spargers, closely paralleling the geometry of stainless steel stirred-tank bioreactors. This geometric consistency supports scale-up translation using the same dimensionless criteria applied to stainless steel scale-up. Downstream integration in a single-use facility Downstream processing in a single-use biomanufacturing facility connects the harvest from the production bioreactor to the purified drug substance through a sequence of unit operations, most of which can now be implemented with single-use flow paths, filter assemblies, and holding vessels. Harvest and primary clarification typically use depth filtration with single-use filter capsule assemblies, followed by sterile filtration into a single-use holding bag. Ultrafiltration and diafiltration (UF/DF) for concentration and buffer exchange use single-use tangential flow filtration cassette systems mounted in single-use flow path holders. Buffer and media preparation uses single-use mixing bags at volumes from 50 to 3,000 liters, eliminating the CIP requirements of stainless steel mixing tanks. Continue reading below... Read More The downstream component that has been slowest to transition to fully single-use formats is large-scale chromatography. Protein A affinity capture, the standard first purification step for monoclonal antibodies, can be performed in single-use column formats at clinical scale, but large-scale single-use chromatography systems remain technically and economically limited compared to stainless steel column formats at commercial production volumes. For facilities planning for the long-term evolution of downstream processing technology, the related coverage of purification breakthroughs promising faster biologic development provides context on emerging approaches that may change this calculus. Drug substance storage between downstream unit operations and at the end of the purification process uses single-use bags in 2-dimensional or 3-dimensional formats, held at 2 to 8 degrees Celsius for short-term hold or frozen in controlled-rate freezers for long-term storage at -80 degrees Celsius. Single-use bag integrity at freeze-thaw cycles is a qualification consideration that must be addressed during facility commissioning. Commissioning and qualification timelines The commissioning timeline advantage of single-use facilities is one of the most frequently cited arguments for the platform, and the advantage is real. Eliminating CIP/SIP systems removes the installation, qualification, and cleaning validation work that represents weeks to months of commissioning time in stainless steel facilities. A well-planned single-use facility can move from equipment delivery to first GMP production run in 12 to 18 months less than an equivalent stainless steel facility. Qualification of single-use equipment follows the same IQ/OQ/PQ framework that applies to all GMP production equipment. The hardware platform, including the bioreactor controller, drive system, sensors, and process piping connections, requires full IQ/OQ/PQ qualification. Bag integrity testing for each individual production bag, confirming the absence of leaks before inoculation, is a per-run pre-use check rather than a qualification activity, but the procedure for conducting it must be established during qualification. Leachables and extractables (L&E) testing is a commissioning requirement specific to single-use systems. All product-contact single-use components must be characterized for chemical entities that can leach from the plastic into the drug substance under process conditions. Major bioprocessing equipment suppliers publish extractables characterization packages for their single-use component portfolios, but sponsors are responsible for demonstrating that the extractables profile of each component is compatible with their specific drug substance under their specific process conditions. The regulatory expectations of FDA biologics guidances and EMA guidelines for biologics manufacturing both require that single-use system L&E data be included in regulatory submissions for biologic drug products. The regulatory consequences of inadequate CMC documentation for biomanufacturing facilities, including single-use facilities, are well-established. Analysis of FDA complete response letters shows that manufacturing and quality deficiencies, including facility readiness gaps, are among the most common reasons for application rejection. For the better part of five decades, stainless steel was the only credible architecture for commercial biopharmaceutical manufacturing. Fixed vessels, welded piping, clean-in-place and steam-in-place infrastructure, and facility timelines measured in years were simply the cost of entry into GMP production. The capital requirements were prohibitive for all but the most well-capitalized manufacturers, and the facilities that existed were built to run a single product at high volume for the lifetime of a commercial approval.
The economics have shifted fundamentally. For facilities targeting clinical and early commercial scale, manufacturing multiple products across a shared infrastructure, or responding to the compressed timelines of modern drug development, single-use architecture has become the default design choice. The question for most new biopharmaceutical facility projects is no longer whether to use single-use technology, but how to design a facility that maximizes what single-use makes possible.
The transition to single-use carries real and measurable operational advantages: lower capital commitment, faster commissioning, superior multi-product flexibility, and the elimination of cleaning validation as an ongoing operational burden. It also creates design requirements, supply chain obligations, and regulatory considerations specific to the disposable format. This guide covers the architecture, qualification approach, and operational design of a well-executed single-use biomanufacturing facility. Download PDF Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) What is a single-use biomanufacturing facility? A single-use biomanufacturing facility is a GMP pharmaceutical production facility in which the equipment that contacts the drug substance during manufacturing, including bioreactor vessels, tubing, filters, mixing containers, and storage bags, uses disposable components that are replaced with each production run rather than cleaned and reused. Single-use facilities eliminate the need for clean-in-place and steam-in-place systems and the cleaning validation required for stainless steel equipment, offering lower capital cost, faster commissioning, and greater flexibility for multi-product manufacturing. How does a single-use facility compare to a stainless steel facility in terms of cost? Single-use facilities require significantly lower upfront capital investment than equivalent stainless steel facilities, primarily because they eliminate the cost of CIP/SIP systems, stainless steel vessel fabrication, and GMP piping infrastructure. They also commission 12 to 18 months faster. The trade-off is higher ongoing operational expenditure: bags, tubing sets, filters, and sterile connectors are replaced with each production run, creating a consumables cost that accumulates over time. For clinical-scale and early commercial facilities, the capital savings and commissioning speed of single-use typically outweigh the consumables cost premium. Feb 18, 2026 | 2 min read credit: istock.com/Noctiluxx Download PDF ATLANTA, GA, February 18th, 2026 --( BUSINESS WIRE )--Axion BioSystems today announced that the FDA's Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER) has accepted the company’s letter of intent (LOI) into the Innovative Science and Technology Approaches for New Drugs (ISTAND) Program for its Human iPSC-Cardiomyocyte MEA Assay for Prediction of Clinical Cardiovascular Repolarization Risk. The submission represents the first stem cell-derived, functional cardiac safety assay accepted into the ISTAND program. The ISTAND program is designed to advance promising, high-impact New Approach Methodologies (NAMs) through structured FDA engagement to inform regulatory decision-making. Acceptance of Axion’s LOI reflects the FDA’s interest in advancing mature, human-relevant, non-animal strategies that can strengthen early assessment of clinical cardiac risk. Cardiac safety remains a major challenge, contributing both to late-stage failures and, in some cases, the premature discontinuation of otherwise promising therapies. The proposed assay combines human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes (hiPSC-CMs) with Axion’s Maestro multielectrode array (MEA) technology to measure cardiac electrophysiology across a multicellular network, or syncytium. Using label-free, noninvasive recordings, the assay enables detection of delayed repolarization, beat-to-beat variability, and arrhythmia-like events associated with proarrhythmic risk — providing human-relevant functional insight beyond single-ion-channel or animal-based approaches. Standardized implementation of the assay is enabled by Axion’s Maestro MEA platform, a widely adopted electrophysiology tool designed to support scalable, reproducible workflows in pharmaceutical and CRO environments. Maestro enables simultaneous recording across up to 96 wells with integrated environmental control, automation-ready operation, and multimodal capabilities. These features support consistent application of the hiPSC-CM MEA assay in regulatory-facing cardiac safety evaluations intended to inform decision-making. “Acceptance into the FDA’s ISTAND Program is an important milestone, not just for Axion BioSystems, but for the broader movement toward human-relevant cardiac safety assessment,” said Julien Bradley , CEO of Axion BioSystems. “This assay reflects more than a decade of scientific validation, collaborative studies, and real-world use across industry and regulatory settings. We look forward to working with FDA to advance its qualification as a drug development tool that can increase confidence in early cardiac safety decisions.” Axion has long played a key role in advancing functional cardiac safety assays, including participation in multicenter initiatives such as the Comprehensive in vitro Proarrhythmia Assay (CiPA). These efforts helped demonstrate that hiPSC-cardiomyocyte MEA assays can reliably identify delayed repolarization and arrhythmia-like events associated with torsades de pointes risk, contributing to their growing use in regulatory-facing drug development programs. As part of the ISTAND program, Axion BioSystems will engage with FDA to develop a Qualification Plan defining the assay’s context of use, analytical validation strategy, and supporting evidence. Qualification of the assay as a DDT may enable broader regulatory acceptance of stem cell-derived functional cardiac safety data across drug development programs. articles.title: From 5L to 5000L: the engineering behind seamless bioreactor scale-up
articles.text:
Articles From 5L to 5000L: the engineering behind seamless bioreactor scale-up Scaling up used to mean starting over. With consistent geometry and mixing design, bench-to-commercial bioreactor translation is becoming predictable. Written by Trevor J Henderson Trevor J Henderson Trevor Henderson is the Creative Services Director for the Laboratory Products Group at LabX Media Group. With over two decades of experience, he specializes in scientific and technical writing, editing, View Full Profile Learn about our Editorial Policies . Jun 4, 2026 | 7 min read The challenge of bioreactor scale-up is not biological: cells do not know how large the vessel around them is. The challenge is hydrodynamic. Maintaining consistent oxygen transfer, mixing uniformity, and shear stress profiles as vessel volume increases by three orders of magnitude is the engineering problem that scale-up criteria, geometric design, and scale-down modeling are all built to solve. Flow (2026) Download PDF Register for free to listen to this article Listen with Speechify 0:00 7:00 Highlights in this article Why scale-up fails: the physics of increasing volume The engineering criteria of bioreactor scale-up Geometric similarity: engineering predictability into the vessel design Scale-down models: predicting commercial behavior at bench scale N-1 perfusion: redefining the inoculation density Process analytical technology in scale-up verification Most bioreactor scale-up failures are not scientific failures. They are engineering failures. The biology that worked at 5 liters, including the cell line, the media, the feeding strategy, and the dissolved oxygen setpoint, is sound. What changes between the bench bioreactor and the 2,000-liter production vessel is the physics of the environment surrounding those cells, and if those changes are not anticipated and engineered for, the process that looked excellent at small scale will behave unexpectedly at large scale. The parameters that govern cell culture productivity do not scale linearly with volume. Mixing time, oxygen transfer rate, CO2 accumulation, and shear stress distribution all change in ways that can stress cells, alter product quality attributes, and create batch-to-batch variability that raises regulatory questions. Understanding how and why these parameters change and designing scale-up strategies to control them is the technical foundation of predictable scale-up. This article covers the engineering principles of bioreactor scale-up, from the dimensionless criteria used to design consistent hydrodynamic environments to the role of N-1 perfusion in redefining inoculation density. For the facility design context in which this scale-up engineering operates, see the blueprint for single-use biomanufacturing facilities , and for the broader bioprocessing lifecycle from development through commercial manufacturing, see the ultimate guide to bioprocessing scale-up and Pharma 4.0 . Continue reading below... Articles Improving HLA-informed cell therapy development Explore engineered cellular models and screening approaches designed to support more targeted evaluation of adoptive cell therapies. Read More Why scale-up fails: the physics of increasing volume When a bioreactor volume increases by a factor of 1,000, from 5 liters to 5,000 liters, the linear dimensions of the vessel increase by only the cube root of 1,000, approximately 10-fold. That geometric relationship governs everything about how the hydrodynamics of the culture change, and most of those changes make the engineering problem harder. Mixing time, the time required for a pulse addition to be uniformly distributed throughout the vessel, increases with scale under constant volumetric power input. In a 5-liter bioreactor, a base pulse from the pH control loop may homogenize in seconds. In a 2,000-liter vessel, the same pulse may create a transient pH gradient that exposes cells in the vicinity of the addition point to conditions outside the setpoint range for tens of seconds before bulk mixing restores uniformity. Cells exposed to repeated pH excursions can shift glycosylation patterns and charge variant profiles, potentially affecting critical quality attributes of the drug substance. Dissolved CO2 accumulation is another scale-dependent challenge. In large-scale bioreactors, the hydrostatic pressure at the bottom of a tall vessel increases the partial pressure of dissolved CO2 beyond levels typically encountered at bench scale, and bubbles have a longer residence time in the culture as they rise through a deeper liquid column. Elevated pCO2 can inhibit cell growth and alter glycosylation, and the CO2 stripping strategy that works at 5 liters may be insufficient at 2,000 liters. Shear stress distribution also changes. Impeller tip speed, which correlates with the shear forces cells experience near the agitator, scales with impeller diameter and rotation speed. Maintaining a constant tip speed at large scale while also maintaining adequate mixing requires impeller design choices that become increasingly complex as vessel volume increases. Research published in Biotechnology Progress in 2025 confirmed that hydrodynamic conditions, including volumetric power input, impeller configuration, and aeration strategy, are among the most significant determinants of production yield during CHO fed-batch scale-up, and that no single criterion adequately captures the full complexity of the scale-up problem. The engineering criteria of bioreactor scale-up Scale-up engineering uses dimensionless or volume-normalized criteria to design bioreactor operating conditions that maintain consistent hydrodynamic environments as vessel scale increases. No single criterion perfectly captures the full complexity of scale-up, and in practice, scale-up engineers must choose which criterion to prioritize based on the process requirements and the cell line's specific sensitivities. Criterion What it controls How it is maintained Key trade-off at large scale P/V (volumetric power input) Mixing energy per unit volume; shear stress distribution Constant agitation power per unit volume as vessel scale increases Maintaining P/V at large scale requires higher tip speeds, increasing shear stress risk for sensitive cell lines kLa (oxygen transfer coefficient) Rate of oxygen delivery from gas to culture; critical at high viable cell density Combined adjustment of agitation rate, sparge gas flow, and sparger design to maintain target kLa Higher gas flows increase foaming and CO2 stripping; bubble coalescence behavior changes with vessel geometry Tip speed Local shear near impeller blade; primary shear stress experienced by cells Constant impeller peripheral velocity across scales Conflicts with P/V criterion at large scale; requires impeller diameter and geometry optimization Mixing time (tm) Time for complete homogenization; determines pH and DO gradient severity Geometric similarity and optimized impeller configuration Inherently increases with volume; spatial heterogeneity in large bioreactors can affect critical quality attributes vvm (volumetric gas flow rate) Total gas delivery per unit culture volume; CO2 stripping capacity Constant gas volume per culture volume per minute CO2 accumulates with increasing vessel height; bubble behavior changes with hydrostatic pressure at depth In practice, maintaining constant P/V is the most widely used primary scale-up criterion for mammalian cell culture because it most directly controls the mixing environment and is most predictive of cell culture performance. kLa is typically verified as a secondary criterion to confirm adequate oxygen delivery at the target agitation and gassing conditions. Tip speed is monitored as a constraint: if the tip speed required to maintain P/V at large scale exceeds the shear sensitivity threshold of the cell line, the impeller design must be revised. Continue reading below... Articles DNA synthesis 101: steps, enzymes, and importance Explore the principles, technologies, and applications that enable scientists to design and build DNA for research, biotechnology, and therapeutic development. Read More Geometric similarity: engineering predictability into the vessel design The most reliable foundation for predictable scale-up is geometric similarity across the full volume range of a bioreactor platform. When key geometric ratios, including the height-to-diameter ratio of the vessel (H/D), the ratio of impeller diameter to tank diameter (d/D), and the impeller off-bottom clearance, are held constant from 5 liters to 5,000 liters, the dimensionless hydrodynamic behavior of the culture scales predictably. The kLa, mixing time, and shear profiles calculated or measured at bench scale will translate to large scale without requiring empirical re-optimization of every operating parameter. This principle is why modern single-use bioreactor platforms designed for process development through commercial manufacturing maintain consistent geometric ratios across their volume range. A development bioreactor and a production bioreactor from the same platform family, operating at the same impeller rotation speed in revolutions per minute per liter of culture, will produce similar hydrodynamic environments because the geometry that generates those environments is consistent. Scale-up becomes a matter of calculating the correct operating parameters for the new volume, rather than re-characterizing the process from scratch. For single-use bioreactors, bag geometry is as important as vessel geometry. The working volume fraction of the bag, the aspect ratio of the inflated bag at maximum fill, and the film architecture, meaning the layered polymer construction of the bag itself, affect both the hydrodynamic environment inside the vessel and the extractables profile of the bag material in contact with the drug substance. Consistent film specifications across a platform's volume range are a prerequisite for assuming that extractables data generated at small scale will be representative of large-scale production conditions. Scale-down models: predicting commercial behavior at bench scale Designing a scale-down model that accurately predicts the behavior of a large-scale production bioreactor is one of the most valuable investments a process development team can make. A 2025 study published in the Journal of Biological Engineering documented successful scale-up of CHO cell cultures across three orders of magnitude, from 96-well microtiter plates through stirred-tank bioreactors, by carefully matching oxygen transfer rates and mixing conditions at each scale. The study confirmed that oxygen transfer rate, not simply agitation speed, is the critical parameter for maintaining cell culture performance across scale transitions. A scale-down model for a 2,000-liter production bioreactor is typically a 10- to 15-liter bioreactor operated to mimic the kLa, mixing time, and pH and DO control dynamics of the large-scale vessel. For processes sensitive to pH heterogeneity, scale-down heterogeneity models deliberately introduce controlled pH or dissolved oxygen gradients that simulate the transient excursions cells experience in a large vessel where base pulses do not distribute instantaneously. These models allow process development scientists to evaluate the impact of large-scale heterogeneity on cell performance and product quality without consuming the time and resources of a full-scale run. Continue reading below... Infographics How to run a successful high-throughput screening campaign Learn the key assay design principles and workflow considerations that help support robust, scalable, and reliable high-throughput screening campaigns. Read More Miniaturized bioreactor systems operating at 15 to 250 milliliters enable high-throughput screening of operating conditions, cell lines, and media formulations with consistent hydrodynamic control in a parallel format. These systems are most valuable in early process development, where large numbers of conditions must be evaluated quickly. Their role in scale-up validation is more limited: they can confirm parameter sensitivity and establish media and feeding optima, but a 15-milliliter vessel cannot faithfully reproduce the CO2 accumulation and mixing time dynamics of a 2,000-liter production bioreactor. N-1 perfusion: redefining the inoculation density Conventional fed-batch bioreactor scale-up begins with inoculation at a viable cell density of approximately 0.5 million cells per milliliter. The culture then spends the first three to five days of the production run in a growth phase, building cell density before peak productivity is reached. That growth phase consumes bioreactor time, media, and production capacity without generating product, and any variability in the health or density of the seed material propagates directly into production bioreactor performance. N-1 perfusion changes this starting point. By running the final seed train stage in perfusion mode, continuously exchanging spent media with fresh media while retaining cells in the vessel, the N-1 bioreactor can accumulate viable cell density far beyond what is achievable in a standard batch seed. Research from Bristol Myers Squibb published in Bioengineering in 2022 demonstrated that N-1 perfusion with in-line capacitance probe control achieved 4.5-fold higher inoculation VCD than conventional batch N-1 seeding, delivering 2 to 10 million cells per milliliter to the production bioreactor versus the standard 0.5 million cells per milliliter. The production consequences are significant. A production bioreactor inoculated at 2 to 10 million cells per milliliter bypasses the slow growth phase, reaching peak viable cell density faster, maintaining higher peak VCD for longer, and generating proportionally more product in the same calendar time. A 2024 study published in Biotechnology Progress demonstrated that N-1 perfusion-enabled high inoculation density processes achieved an average 85% titer increase and 132% space-time yield increase compared to conventional low-inoculation-density fed-batch processes across six CHO cell lines expressing three different monoclonal antibodies. Integrating N-1 perfusion into scale-up design also improves the uniformity of seed material delivered to the production bioreactor, reducing run-to-run variability that can otherwise be attributed to variation in the physiological state of the inoculum rather than to true process variability at production scale. Process analytical technology in scale-up verification Process analytical technology (PAT) bridges the bench and commercial scale by providing real-time, in-process measurements of the critical parameters that scale-up engineering is designed to control. The FDA's PAT framework guidance , first published in 2004, explicitly supports the use of real-time quality monitoring rather than end-product testing and encouraged manufacturers to build process understanding through in-line and on-line measurement systems. That regulatory support has enabled the adoption of a generation of PAT tools that are now routinely deployed in both scale-down models and production bioreactors. Continue reading below... Application Note Scaling neuronal activity profiling with semi-automated electrophysiology Advanced microelectrode array and liquid handling technologies make neuronal culture screening more consistent and easier to scale. Read More In scale-up verification, PAT serves two complementary functions. At small scale, it establishes multivariate models that correlate measured process signals with cell culture performance and product quality outcomes. At large scale, it confirms that the critical process parameters defined during small-scale development are being maintained within their designed ranges, and that the performance the models predict at small scale is actually being achieved at production scale. Key PAT tools in bioreactor scale-up verification include in-line Raman spectroscopy for real-time glucose, lactate, and product concentration measurement; near-infrared spectroscopy for cell density and metabolite monitoring; and capacitance probes for viable cell density estimation without sampling. The integration of multiple PAT data streams into a unified process monitoring platform enables real-time decisions about feeding, pH adjustment, and harvest timing that would otherwise depend on discrete offline measurements taken hours apart. For context on how PAT and digital manufacturing tools integrate into the broader Pharma 4.0 framework, see the related coverage in the ultimate guide to bioprocessing scale-up and Pharma 4.0 . For the role of purification and downstream scale-up as the continuation of the upstream scale-up engineering challenge, see the coverage of purification breakthroughs promising faster biologic development . This article was produced under Drug Discovery News' AI Editorial Guidelines Download PDF Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) What is bioreactor scale-up? Bioreactor scale-up is the process of translating a cell culture manufacturing process from a small development-scale bioreactor to progressively larger vessels, ultimately reaching commercial production scale. The goal is to maintain the same hydrodynamic environment, including oxygen transfer rate, mixing uniformity, and shear stress distribution, at each larger scale so that cell culture performance and product quality attributes are preserved. Scale-up spans from bench-scale bioreactors of 5 to 15 liters in early development through clinical-scale vessels of 50 to 500 liters and production-scale vessels of 500 to 5,000 liters. What scale-up criteria are used to design consistent bioreactor environments? The most commonly used scale-up criteria in mammalian cell culture are volumetric power input (P/V), which maintains consistent mixing energy per unit volume; the oxygen transfer coefficient (kLa), which maintains consistent oxygen delivery; and tip speed, which maintains consistent shear stress near the impeller. Mixing time is monitored as a key outcome of the design, and volumetric gas flow rate (vvm) is maintained to ensure adequate CO2 stripping. No single criterion perfectly captures all aspects of scale-up, and process engineers must balance these criteria based on the specific sensitivities of their cell line and process. Why does pH become heterogeneous in large-scale bioreactors? In large-scale bioreactors, the base solution added by the pH control loop takes time to distribute throughout the vessel after each pulse addition. During that mixing time, the region near the addition point experiences a transient pH elevation before bulk mixing restores uniformity. In a 5-liter bioreactor, mixing may be complete in seconds. In a 2,000-liter vessel, mixing time under equivalent volumetric power input is longer, creating more significant and more prolonged pH gradients. Cells repeatedly exposed to these transient excursions can experience physiological stress that shifts glycosylation patterns and charge variant profiles, affecting critical quality attributes of the drug substance. What is N-1 perfusion and how does it improve bioreactor scale-up? N-1 perfusion runs the final stage of the seed train in perfusion mode, continuously exchanging spent media for fresh media while retaining cells in the vessel, allowing the seed culture to accumulate viable cell densities of 20 to 80 million cells per milliliter before inoculating the production bioreactor. Conventional batch N-1 seeding delivers inoculation densities of approximately 0.5 million cells per milliliter to the production bioreactor. N-1 perfusion has been shown to enable inoculation at 2 to 10 million cells per milliliter, a four- to 20-fold improvement that shortens the production bioreactor growth phase, increases peak viable cell density, and improves volumetric productivity. Published studies report titer increases of 85% or more from N-1 perfusion-enabled high inoculation density processes. What makes a good scale-down model for a production bioreactor? A good scale-down model matches the key hydrodynamic parameters of the large-scale production bioreactor, including kLa, mixing time, and the CO2 stripping characteristics of the gassing system, at a volume small enough to run in parallel with other development experiments. Beyond basic hydrodynamic matching, effective scale-down models for large-scale processes often incorporate deliberate pH or dissolved oxygen gradients that simulate the heterogeneity cells experience in large vessels, allowing development scientists to evaluate the impact of large-scale mixing limitations on cell performance and product quality without conducting a full-scale run. How does geometric similarity support bioreactor scale-up? Geometric similarity means maintaining consistent ratios of key vessel dimensions, including the vessel height-to-diameter ratio, the ratio of impeller diameter to vessel diameter, and impeller clearance from the vessel bottom, across all scales of a bioreactor platform. When these ratios are held constant, the dimensionless hydrodynamic behavior of the culture scales predictably with volume. The kLa, mixing time, and shear profiles at bench scale translate reliably to large scale, and operating conditions for new volumes can be calculated rather than empirically re-characterized from scratch. This is why bioreactor platforms designed with consistent geometry across their volume range provide more predictable scale-up than platforms where geometry varies by scale. Jun 4, 2026 | 7 min read The challenge of bioreactor scale-up is not biological: cells do not know how large the vessel around them is. The challenge is hydrodynamic. Maintaining consistent oxygen transfer, mixing uniformity, and shear stress profiles as vessel volume increases by three orders of magnitude is the engineering problem that scale-up criteria, geometric design, and scale-down modeling are all built to solve. They are engineering failures. The biology that worked at 5 liters, including the cell line, the media, the feeding strategy, and the dissolved oxygen setpoint, is sound. What changes between the bench bioreactor and the 2,000-liter production vessel is the physics of the environment surrounding those cells, and if those changes are not anticipated and engineered for, the process that looked excellent at small scale will behave unexpectedly at large scale. The parameters that govern cell culture productivity do not scale linearly with volume. Mixing time, oxygen transfer rate, CO2 accumulation, and shear stress distribution all change in ways that can stress cells, alter product quality attributes, and create batch-to-batch variability that raises regulatory questions. Understanding how and why these parameters change and designing scale-up strategies to control them is the technical foundation of predictable scale-up. This article covers the engineering principles of bioreactor scale-up, from the dimensionless criteria used to design consistent hydrodynamic environments to the role of N-1 perfusion in redefining inoculation density.
